glossary.entries.consistency.body.0: A proof system that never proves both a sentence and its negation has consistency. An inconsistent one proves everything, by principle of explosion, and so says nothing. A sound system is consistent; not always the other way: consistency only asks that it not contradict itself, not that what it proves be true.
glossary.entries.consistency.title: consistency
glossary.entries.constructor.body.0: The symbols that make the values of an are its constructors: 0 and S for numbers, [] and # for lists. Every value of the type is made by them, and in only one way: so \(0\neq S\) x, and S a = S b gives a = b.
glossary.entries.constructor.title: constructor
glossary.entries.defeq.body.0: Before comparing two types, the kernel computes (unfolding definitions, putting in arguments, β-reduction), and what comes out alike counts as alike: definitional equality. 1 + 1 = 2 and 0 + x = x are proved by rfl, and a proof’s type can be read through it too. Which equalities are definitional depends on how the definitions are written.
glossary.entries.defeq.title: definitional equality
glossary.entries.dependent.body.0: A dependent type is a type that depends on a value: Vec n is vectors n long. In a function such as “\(\forall x.\, \text{Vec x}\to \text{Vec}\; (S\; x)\)”, the type of the result depends on the argument. With the length in the type, a mistake such as taking the first of an empty vector is refused when types are checked.
glossary.entries.dependent.body.1: In Lean, proofs of the same proposition in Prop are considered equal (proof irrelevance). Values in Type, such as numbers, lists and vectors, can be used in computations.
glossary.entries.dependent.title: Dependent types
glossary.entries.goedel-coding.body.0: Give each symbol a number, and code a sentence’s symbols in order as one number: a sentence becomes a number, and so does a proof, a list of sentences. Then “x numbers a proof” and “the sentence numbered x can be proved” become sentences about numbers, and arithmetic can speak of its own proofs. Programs are coded as numbers the same way: the ⟨y⟩ of the halting problem is one.
glossary.entries.goedel-coding.title: Gödel numbering
glossary.entries.implicit.body.0: An implicit parameter can be inferred from other arguments or from the expected type. Lean writes it as {x : nat} and fills it in by unification. Isabelle does the same by type inference.
glossary.entries.implicit.title: implicit argument
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.0: The first incompleteness theorem applies to consistent, effectively axiomatized theories strong enough for elementary arithmetic: such a theory has an arithmetic sentence it can neither prove nor refute. The classical argument uses and diagonal argument to construct a sentence about its own provability, an idea related to the The liar. The truth and possible refutability of a particular sentence depend on the construction and additional assumptions.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.1: The second incompleteness theorem: a consistent, effectively axiomatized theory strong enough for arithmetic and satisfying suitable derivability conditions cannot prove its standard formalized consistency statement. The precise conclusion depends on the theory and consistency statement.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.body.2: This does not conflict with first-order completeness: logical completeness concerns validity across all structures, whereas incompleteness concerns what a particular arithmetic theory can prove. Adding an independent sentence can settle that sentence, but an extension meeting the same conditions still has independent sentences.
glossary.entries.incompleteness.title: incompleteness theorem
glossary.entries.induction.body.0: To prove something for every number, prove it for 0, then prove that whenever it holds for x it holds for S x: this is induction. Every has an induction rule of its own, a premise per constructor, with an induction hypothesis for each argument of its own type. When Simp is stuck because x is not known to be made by one constructor or another, it is time for induction.
glossary.entries.induction.title: induction
glossary.entries.inductive.body.0: A type built up layer by layer from a few constructors is an inductive type: nat = 0 | S nat, list = [] | x # xs. The declaration says only that, and the prover supplies a set of rules: values made by different constructors differ, values made by one constructor are equal only if their arguments are, cases, induction, and functions defined by recursion over the constructors. Isabelle’s datatype and Lean’s inductive are such declarations.
glossary.entries.inductive.title: inductive type
glossary.entries.injectivity.body.0: Two values made by the same are equal only if their arguments are: S a = S b gives a = b, and x # xs = y # ys gives x = y and xs = ys. This is the injectivity of constructors. Together with “different constructors differ” it says every value is made in exactly one way.
glossary.entries.injectivity.title: One-to-one
glossary.entries.ordered.body.0: A rule like x + y = y + x, whose sides differ only in where the variables go, makes a The simplifier go round in circles. Ordered rewriting fixes an order on expressions and uses the rule only when the result is “smaller”. Isabelle’s simp does this for such rules automatically, so commutativity can go into Simp.
glossary.entries.ordered.title: ordered rewriting
glossary.entries.propeq.body.0: x + 0 = x is true, but addition recurses on its first number, and with x unknown the kernel gets stuck: it takes induction, a propositional equality. Using it to replace part of a type takes ▸; a needs nothing written, since the kernel computes it. Isabelle’s HOL has no layer of definitional equality: every equality is proved by rules or worked out by the simplifier.
glossary.entries.propeq.title: propositional equality
glossary.entries.transport.body.0: When lengths in types do not compute to the same, a value has to be transported across an equation: h ▸ v is the same vector under an equal length. This is the price of a ; Lean’s libraries often rewrite a definition just so the equality needed becomes definitional.
glossary.entries.transport.title: transport
level.decl-bool.after: Every “if” in a program is, in a proof, a split into cases on a truth value.
level.decl-bool.intro.0.t: The result of a comparison is not a sentence but a value: true or false. They too are a kind of thing that is declared.
level.decl-bool.tasks.decl-bool.brief: Requirement: true needs nothing, false needs nothing, and they are two different things. Write the declaration of truth values.
level.decl-bool.tasks.decl-bool.hint.0: How much does each of true and false need?
level.decl-bool.title: Declaring true and false
level.decl-list.intro.0.t: A list is a row of things: the empty one [], or a thing put in front of a list, written x :: xs.
level.decl-list.tasks.decl-list.brief: Requirement: a list can be made from nothing (the empty list); taking any thing and a list, the list with that thing in front can be made. Write the declaration of lists.
level.decl-list.tasks.decl-list.hint.0: The second way needs two things: a thing, and a list.
level.decl-list.title: Declaring lists
level.decl-nat.after: A type declared this way is an <wiki-ref to="qed-math/inductive"></wiki-ref>. The kernel makes three kinds of rule from it: cases, induction, and the constructors all being different.
level.decl-nat.intro.0.t: Why is every natural number zero or the successor of another number? Declare the natural numbers, then use the rules the declaration gives you in computations and proofs.
level.decl-nat.intro.1.t: Numbers too come from a declaration. This time what is declared is a kind of thing, and its introduction rules are called <wiki-ref to="qed-math/constructor"></wiki-ref>s: each makes a number.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.brief: Requirement: a number can be made from nothing (0); given a number, the next one can be made. Write the declaration of the numbers.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.hint.0: The requirement names two ways to make one.
level.decl-nat.tasks.decl-nat.hint.1: The premise of the second way is a number itself.
level.decl-nat.title: Declaring the numbers
level.def-list.intro.0.t: Define two functions on lists: append and length.
level.def-list.tasks.def-list-1.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.def-list.tasks.def-list-1.hint.0: In x :: xs followed by ys, x is still in front.
xs ++ ys joins two lists; the one it takes apart is the first.
level.def-list.tasks.def-list-2.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.def-list.title: Defining append and length
level.def-max.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="qed-math/decl-bool"></level-ref> brought true and false. Define comparison first, then the larger of two with it.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-1.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-1.hint.0: Taking one S off each side leaves the comparison as it was.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-1.intro.0.t: \(x\le y\) is true or false. Both numbers are taken apart, so there are three rows: 0 against any number, S x against 0, S x against S y.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-2.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-2.hint.0: Look for the row whose condition says x is no bigger than y.
level.def-max.tasks.def-max-2.intro.0.t: max takes no number apart; it looks at whether \(x\le y\) is true: one row for true, one for false, each with a condition.
level.def-max.title: Comparing, and the larger
level.def-plus.after: Lean compiles such a definition into the recursor of the numbers, Nat.rec.
level.def-plus.intro.0.t: There are numbers, but no addition yet. To define a function, write one row for each constructor of the number it takes apart: what 0 + y is, and what S x + y is. A right side may use addition again, but only on a smaller number, or it never finishes.
level.def-plus.tasks.def-plus.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.def-plus.tasks.def-plus.hint.0: S x + y is one more than x + y.
level.def-plus.title: Defining addition
level.demo-anc.after: A declaration whose own sentence appears among its premises is an inductive declaration. It still says “only these ways”: starting from the parents on record, only what these two rules build round after round counts as an ancestor, so siblings do not. The elimination rule under the table has one more premise, R(z, y): the induction hypothesis, which comes from the premise “z is an ancestor of y”. Lean writes this declaration as an inductive, with one constructor for each derivable situation.
level.demo-anc.intro.0.t: The premises in the declarations of “and” and “or” were other sentences. The sentence declared here relates two people, and it may appear among its own premises.
level.demo-anc.intro.1.t: The first row of the rule board is the sentence being declared, for any x and y. Each derivable situation may also take any z.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-strong.bri: Write one test case that exposes this declaration: the conclusion is not derivable by the requirement, but this declaration derives it.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-strong.hin: Try two children of the same person.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-strong.int: Another declaration writes the second way as: z is a parent of x, and z is an ancestor of y.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-weak.brief: Write one test case that exposes this declaration: the conclusion is derivable by the requirement, but this declaration cannot derive it.
The requirement says “through any number of generations”.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-weak.intro: Someone translated the requirement as: parents are ancestors, and so are grandparents.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-write.brie: Requirement: the family record only says who is a parent of whom. A person’s ancestors are their parents, their parents’ parents, and so on upward through any number of generations; nobody else counts. Write the declaration of “x is an ancestor of y”.
level.demo-anc.tasks.demo-anc-write.hint: The requirement gives two ways: one generation apart, and more than one.
With more generations between them there is always someone z in the middle: x is a parent of z, and z is already an ancestor of y.
level.demo-anc.title: Demo · Declare ancestor
level.demo-nat.after: The premise of the second way is “natural number” itself, so the generated elimination rule gives one more R in that case: the result already obtained for the number in hand. That is the induction hypothesis.
level.demo-nat.intro.0.t: This time the declaration is of a kind of thing. The requirement only says what it is for; finding the ways to build it is up to you.
level.demo-nat.tasks.demo-nat.brief: Requirement: something to count with. Having counted nothing is already a number; counting one more gives the next number from the one in hand; there are no numbers other than those counted this way. Write the declaration of the natural numbers.
level.demo-nat.tasks.demo-nat.hint.0: The requirement gives two ways to get a number.
level.demo-nat.tasks.demo-nat.hint.1: The second way needs a number in hand first.
level.demo-nat.title: Demo · Declare the natural numbers
level.demo-reach.after: “With any number of connections” became a rule that mentions itself. “Flights go one way” needs no rule: a declaration only says what can be built, and nothing else counts.
level.demo-reach.intro.0.t: The same kind of declaration for another requirement. This time no hint says how many ways there are.
level.demo-reach.tasks.demo-reach.brief: Requirement: the timetable lists direct flights only. A traveller wants to know whether one city can be reached from another: a direct flight counts, and so does any number of connections. Flights go one way; without a return flight there is no way back. Write the declaration of “y can be reached from x”.
level.demo-reach.tasks.demo-reach.hint.0: With a connection, first fly direct to some city z.
level.demo-reach.title: Demo · Declare reachable
level.gd-check.after: “A can be proved” thus becomes a sentence about numbers: some number is a proof that passes the check and concludes A. It is written Prov(⌜A⌝).
level.gd-check.intro.0.t: The second step: proofs become numbers too. A proof is a tree whose leaves are axioms and whose forks are each an Apply, as wired on the board; a tree can be coded as a number. Checking a proof looks at two things: every leaf is in the table of axioms, and every Apply fits (the “if A then B” meets just A). The table holds: it rains, it rains \mark{implies} the ground is wet, the ground is wet \mark{implies} the road is slippery.
level.gd-check.tasks.gd-check.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-check.title: Checking a proof is a computation
level.gd-code.after: A list of numbers can be packed into one number (Gödel put each place in the exponent of a prime: 2^a·3^b·5^c …). Facts about sentences thus become facts about numbers.
level.gd-code.intro.0.t: Arithmetic can talk about proofs. First encode sentences as lists of numbers, then do the same for proofs. The first three levels build rewriting circuits for computations. The last three use the results on the proof board.
level.gd-code.intro.1.t: The first step is <wiki-ref to="qed-math/goedel-coding"></wiki-ref>: each symbol stands for a number, it rains 1, the ground is wet 2, \mark{not} 3, \mark{implies} 4. A sentence is written left to right as a list of numbers, with \mark{implies} in front of its two sides, so no brackets are needed. ⌜A⌝ is the code of the sentence A, worked out by four definitions.
level.gd-code.tasks.gd-code.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-code.title: Sentences become numbers
level.gd-con.after: That is the first incompleteness theorem: a consistent prover whose rules can be listed one by one and which can do addition and multiplication has a true sentence it cannot prove. To show \(\lnot G\) cannot be proved either, Gödel needed a stronger condition; Rosser, in 1936, changed the sentence so that consistency alone is enough.
level.gd-con.intro.0.t: The fifth step. <level-ref to="qed-math/gd-true"></level-ref> used soundness, which is too strong: a prover cannot say of itself that what it proves is true. <wiki-ref to="qed-math/consistency"></wiki-ref> is enough: no sentence is provable together with its negation.
level.gd-con.intro.1.t: The first two givens are about what the prover itself can do. The first: the diagonal (<level-ref to="qed-math/gd-diag"></level-ref>) is only a computation, so the prover too works out that \(G\leftrightarrow G\) cannot be proved; if G can be proved, so can “G cannot be proved”. The second: checking a proof is only a computation (<level-ref to="qed-math/gd-check"></level-ref>), so if G has a proof, the prover checks that number and proves “⌜G⌝ is provable”. The third is consistency: “G cannot be proved” and “⌜G⌝ is provable” negate each other, and cannot both be provable.
level.gd-con.tasks.gd-con.brief: From these three givens, prove: G cannot be proved.
level.gd-con.title: Consistency is enough
level.gd-diag.after: This is the diagonal lemma: for any property P(□) there is a sentence G equivalent to P(⌜G⌝).
level.gd-diag.intro.0.t: The third step makes a sentence that says “I cannot be proved”. The trouble is that a sentence cannot hold its own code: the code is longer than the sentence. Gödel’s way is the diagonal argument: first write a sentence D with a gap □, “the diagonal of □ cannot be proved”. Taking the diagonal is a computation: put a sentence’s own code ⌜…⌝ into its gap.
level.gd-diag.intro.1.t: G is the diagonal of D. The first goal works out G; the second works out the sentence G speaks of (the value of the diagonal of ⌜D⌝).
level.gd-diag.tasks.gd-diag.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.gd-diag.title: The diagonal is a computation
level.gd-second.after: This is the second incompleteness theorem, which ended Hilbert’s programme of proving mathematics consistent by finite means. So proof assistants such as Lean and Isabelle do not prove themselves sound; they keep what must be trusted as small as can be: a little kernel and a few axioms.
level.gd-second.intro.0.t: The last step. ⌜consistent⌝ is a sentence of arithmetic: “no sentence is provable together with its negation”. The first two givens are again what the prover itself can do. The first: the prover can carry out the whole argument of <level-ref to="qed-math/gd-con"></level-ref> (it proves “if consistent, then G cannot be proved”), so proving consistency would prove “G cannot be proved”. The second: it proves “if G cannot be proved, then G” (the diagonal), so proving “G cannot be proved” would prove G. The third is what <level-ref to="qed-math/gd-con"></level-ref> proved.
level.gd-second.tasks.gd-second.brief: From these three givens, prove: “the prover is consistent” cannot be proved.
level.gd-second.title: It cannot prove itself consistent
level.gd-true.after: The liar paradox is about truth and leads to a contradiction. Gödel’s sentence G is about whether it can be proved. Here we derive both G and its unprovability in the original system, the heart of Gödel’s first <wiki-ref to="qed-math/incompleteness"></wiki-ref> theorem.
level.gd-true.intro.0.t: The fourth step. The first two givens come from : G says “the diagonal of ⌜D⌝ cannot be proved”, and the diagonal of ⌜D⌝ works out to ⌜G⌝. Prov comes from : there is a proof that passes the check. In the real theorem Prov must be written as a sentence of arithmetic, with addition and multiplication; that long step is taken as given here. The third given is soundness: what can be proved is true (used here for G alone).
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.brief: From these three givens, prove: G holds, and G cannot be proved.
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.hint.0: The first two givens together relate G to “⌜G⌝ cannot be proved”.
level.gd-true.tasks.gd-true.hint.1: Prove first that G cannot be proved; that G holds follows.
level.gd-true.title: I cannot be proved

level.in-appnil.intro.0.t: The list = [] | x :: xs declared in <level-ref to="qed-math/decl-list"></level-ref> gives the same kinds of rule; its induction steps from xs to x :: xs.

level.in-assoc.tasks.in-assoc.hint.0: Addition’s definition takes apart the number on the left.
level.in-assoc.title: Associativity
level.in-cases.intro.0.t: The declaration’s cases rule reads \mark{open-bracket}t = \(0\Longrightarrow C\); \mark{meta-all}x. t = S \(x\Longrightarrow C\)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} C: to prove C, prove it in each case.
level.in-cases.tasks.in-cases.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-cases.tasks.in-cases.hint.0: If ?t cannot be read off, leave it for a later step to settle.
level.in-cases.title: Zero, or one after
level.in-circle.after: Isabelle fixes an order on expressions and rewrites only towards the smaller, which is called <wiki-ref to="qed-math/ordered"></wiki-ref>.
level.in-circle.tasks.in-circle.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-circle.tasks.in-circle.hint.0: Commutativity in Simp turns x + y into y + x and back again …
level.in-circle.tasks.in-circle.hint.1: After Simp, some goals have both sides the same already, others differ by one swap.
level.in-circle.title: Simp going round in circles
level.in-comm.tasks.in-comm.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-comm.tasks.in-comm.hint.0: Induct on x, and see where each case gets stuck.
level.in-comm.tasks.in-comm.hint.1: Where they get stuck, the “Rule book of numbers” already has equations proved.
level.in-comm.title: Swap
level.in-distinct.intro.0.t: Simp works out 1 + 1, yet cannot prove \(0\neq 1\): no definition says they differ. The declaration does: nat = 0 | S nat of <level-ref to="qed-math/decl-nat"></level-ref> is an <wiki-ref to="qed-math/inductive"></wiki-ref>, and the rules it gives are in the “Rule book of numbers”.
level.in-distinct.tasks.in-distinct.brie: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-distinct.tasks.in-distinct.hint: The “Rule book of numbers” has rules for 0 = S …; one test has its equation the other way round.
level.in-distinct.title: 0 is not 1
level.in-induct.after: This sentence is the elimination rule of the declaration of the numbers. The two-box induction part of <level-ref to="qed-math/in-zero"></level-ref> does just this: choose P, then hand it the two boxes’ conclusions to Apply twice.
level.in-induct.intro.0.t: The declaration in <level-ref to="qed-math/decl-nat"></level-ref> gives one more rule: for every property P, if 0 has P and each n having P gives S n having P, then every number has P. As one sentence: \mark{forall}P. \(P(0)\to (\forall n.\, P(n)\to P(S\; n))\to (\forall n.\, P(n))\).
level.in-induct.intro.1.t: It is a given, used with <part-ref to="part:proof-kit/allE"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="part:proof-kit/mp"></part-ref>: choosing an instance, choose a property to put in for P.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-1.brief: Given induction, 0 + 0 = 0, and for every n that n + 0 = n gives S n + 0 = S n, prove n + 0 = n for every n.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-1.hint.0: In <part-ref to="part:proof-kit/allE"></part-ref> choose the property “x + 0 = x” to put in for P.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-1.hint.1: What it gives needs two things before its conclusion: Apply the two givens in turn.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-2.brief: With induction alone, prove every number is 0 or S of some number.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-2.hint.0: The property is what the goal says of n: “\(x=0\lor (\exists m.\, x=S\; m)\)”.
level.in-induct.tasks.in-induct-2.hint.1: The case 0: reflexivity gives 0 = 0, then introduce \mark{or}. From a to S a: S a = S a is already an example, and the assumption about a is not needed.
level.in-induct.title: Induction is one sentence
level.in-inject.after: The one-to-one proved goes into the “Rule book of numbers”. In Lean’s kernel the same fact is called noConfusion.
level.in-inject.intro.0.t: Two values made by the same constructor are equal only if their arguments are: if S a = S b, then a = b. This is <wiki-ref to="qed-math/injectivity"></wiki-ref>. The declaration does not give it as a rule; it is proved with the help of a function, pred, the number before a number.
level.in-inject.tasks.in-inject-1.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.in-inject.tasks.in-inject-2.brief: From the definition of pred, prove: if S x = S y, then x = y.
level.in-inject.tasks.in-inject-2.hint.0: Take a, and then b, in pred’s definition.
level.in-inject.tasks.in-inject-2.hint.1: The assumed S a = S b can rewrite one of them.
level.in-inject.title: One-to-one
level.in-itsum.intro.0.t: Two sums: one adding from the back, one walking along with an accumulator. Are they the same?
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-1.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-1.hint.0: The sum of x :: xs includes x.
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-2.brief: Write a right side for every row.
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-2.hint.0: At the end, y already holds the sum.
itsum walks along adding each element onto y, and at the end y is the sum. Programmers call this tail recursion.
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-3.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-itsum.tasks.in-itsum-3.hint.0: y changes at each step along.

level.in-loop.intro.0.t: Someone “defines” a function like this: f x = S (f x). The definition board would not take it: working out f 0 needs f 0 first, for ever. What if it were taken?
level.in-loop.tasks.in-loop.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-loop.tasks.in-loop.hint.0: Apply Prove an intermediate claim backwards. Use Never its successor to produce the goal needed for a contradiction, then instantiate the givens.
level.in-loop.tasks.in-loop.hint.1: Apply the implication rule backwards to expose the premises of the contradiction. Finish by citing the givens.

level.in-noteq.intro.0.t: No number is the one after itself: \(x\neq S\) x.
level.in-noteq.tasks.in-noteq.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-noteq.tasks.in-noteq.hint.1: The two cases need the declaration’s rules and the one-to-one proved.
level.in-noteq.title: Never the one after itself

level.in-zero.after: x + 0 = x goes into the “Rule book of numbers”: an equation proved is a rule, and a rewrite rule for Simp.
level.in-zero.intro.0.t: Addition’s definition takes apart only the number on the left. With 0 on the right, particular numbers are easy; for every x, it takes the declaration’s last rule: <wiki-ref to="qed-math/induction"></wiki-ref>.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-1.hint.0: Repeat the rewrites until the two sides match, then apply reflexivity backwards.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-2.brief: From the two definitions of addition, prove x + 0 = x for every x.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-2.hint.0: The case 0 needs only the first definition.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-2.hint.1: From a to S a: the second definition gives S a + 0 = S (a + 0), and the box holds an assumption.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-2.intro.0.t: A new part, “Induction”: choose on it the “for every x” to prove. It has two boxes: the first proves the case 0; in the second there is a number a, the sentence is assumed for a and proved for S a.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-3.brief: Prove x + 0 = x for every x.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-3.hint.0: The induction rule concludes \(\forall x.\, P\)(x), so it can be used backwards.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-3.hint.1: The second goal has an equation among its givens.
level.in-zero.tasks.in-zero-3.intro.0.t: Simp cannot change x + 0: x is not known to be 0 or S of something. The induction rule the declaration gives does what the two-box part does: \mark{open-bracket}P(0); \mark{meta-all}x. P(x) \mark{entails} P(S x)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(\forall x.\, P\)(x).
level.in-zero.title: Zero on the right
level.nl-plus.intro.0.t: On the proof board, the two equations of <level-ref to="qed-math/def-plus"></level-ref>, 0 + y = y and S x + y = S (x + y), are two “for all” givens.
level.nl-plus.tasks.nl-plus.brief: From the two definitions of addition, prove 1 + 1 = 2.
level.nl-plus.tasks.nl-plus.hint.0: Start with <part-ref to="part:proof-kit/allE"></part-ref>, putting particular numbers for the x and y of a definition.
level.nl-plus.tasks.nl-plus.hint.1: The second definition gives S (0 + S 0); the first works out 0 + S 0, which Rewrite then puts in.
level.nl-plus.title: One plus one by hand
level.sort-if.after: The two rules go into the “Rule book of numbers”.
level.sort-if.intro.0.t: if’s definition knows only a true or false written out. When the condition is something like \(c\le a\), Simp cannot tell which it is, and gets stuck. From the definition, prove two rules with a condition: when the condition equals true, take the “then” side; when false, the “else” side.

level.sort-ins.after: Defining a function is writing a program; Simp runs it.
level.sort-ins.intro.0.t: Sorting is a program, and a program can be defined by equations. Insertion sort puts the elements one by one into a sorted list.

level.sp-compute.after: In a proof assistant, computing is rewriting.
level.sp-compute.intro.0.t: Each of addition’s two definition equations is a rewrite rule. Place one card for each equation, join their routes, then repeat until neither equation applies.

level.sp-cond.after: Isabelle’s simplifier calls such rules conditional rewrite rules.
level.sp-cond.intro.0.t: Both rows of max in <level-ref to="qed-math/def-max"></level-ref> carry a condition. Once a rule with a condition rewrites a place, the condition becomes a new goal, queued behind; only when it is proved does the rewrite stand.

level.sp-cond.tasks.sp-cond.hint.0: Which rule for max applies is not known in advance: try both.
level.sp-cond.tasks.sp-cond.hint.1: The way whose condition cannot be proved fails by itself.
level.sp-cond.title: A rule with a condition

part.addAssoc.desc: (x + y) + z = x + (y + z): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.addAssoc.name: Addition associates
part.addComm.desc: x + y = y + x: a rule, and a rewrite rule; in Simp it rewrites back and forth without end.
part.addComm.name: Addition commutes
part.addSucc.desc: x + S y = S (x + y): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.addSucc.name: Add successor
part.addZero.desc: x + 0 = x: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.addZero.name: Add zero
part.appAssoc.desc: (xs ++ ys) ++ zs = xs ++ (ys ++ zs): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.appAssoc.name: Append associates
part.appNil.desc: xs ++ [] = xs: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.appNil.name: Append nil
part.ifFalse.desc: u = false \mark{implies} (if u then v else w) = w: a rule, and a rewrite rule with a condition.
part.ifFalse.name: If false
part.ifTrue.desc: u = true \mark{implies} (if u then v else w) = v: a rule, and a rewrite rule with a condition.
part.ifTrue.name: If true
part.inject.desc: S x = S y \mark{implies} x = y, as a rule that takes apart: when S x = S y is given, the proof goes on from x = y instead.
part.inject.name: One-to-one
part.insLen.desc: len (ins x xs) = S (len xs): a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.insLen.name: Insert adds one
part.revApp.desc: rev (xs ++ ys) = rev ys ++ rev xs: a rule, and a left-to-right rewrite rule for Simp.
part.revApp.name: Reverse of an append
